title: Workers, households, regions: Geographic disparities in labour market outcomes and the distribution of income: OECD Employment Outlook 2026
date_evidence: Local employment and skills OECD Employment Outlook 7 July 2026 Summary Full report Support materials
key_claim: Regional labour-market gaps are large and do not close through people moving. The average within-country employment-rate gap between top- and bottom-quintile regions is 11.4 percentage points; persistently low-employment regions lose only 0.25% of population a year to net internal outmigration while high-employment regions gain roughly 0.15%. The same report finds beta- and sigma-convergence in 21 of 29 countries since the early 2010s.
frame_summary: Where a worker lives determines their labour-market and income chances, and internal migration is far too slow a mechanism to close the resulting regional gaps.
verbatim_quote: People move from low- to high-employment regions, but at a pace much too slow to make labour mobility alone a solution for meaningfully reducing labour market disparities.
verbatim_list: Across countries with available data, regions with persistently low employment – defined as those in the bottom quintile of employment rates within each country for most of the past 15 years – experienced annual net migration outflows of 0.25% of their population; meanwhile, high-employment regions experienced annual net inflows of approximately 0.15% from other parts of the country (see Figure 2.6).

Across OECD economies with comparable data, the average gap in employment rates between high- and low-employment regions – defined as those in the top and bottom quintiles of regions within each country – stands at 11.4 p.p. (Figure 2.1, Panel A).

21 of the 29 countries for which regional employment rates can be traced back to the early 2010s have experienced both catching up by lagging regions (β-convergence) and a narrowing of relative disparities across regions (σ-convergence) (Figure 2.2).
notes: Chapter 2 of the Employment Outlook 2026 (authors Königs, Pinto, Terrero-Dávila, Álvarez Mejía; DOI 10.1787/7e710f54-en). Free, no paywall. The convergence quote in verbatim_list is the counter-evidence used in the Counter-Argument box. Sister chapter component-7 carries the 'adjustment through joblessness and newcomers' finding but has no retrievable date on the live page, so it is not cited.

title: Labour market in the regions of the UK: July 2026
date_evidence: Office for National Statistics (ONS), published 21 July 2026, ONS website, statistical bulletin, Labour market in the regions of the UK: July 2026
key_claim: In March to May 2026 the UK spanned an employment-rate range from 78.2% (South East) to 71.5% (North East), an unemployment range from 6.5% (London) to 1.8% (Northern Ireland), and an inactivity range from 26.5% (Northern Ireland) to 18.5% (South East).
frame_summary: The UK national labour-market aggregate conceals region- and nation-level outcomes that differ by several percentage points at the same moment in time.
verbatim_quote: The highest employment rate in the UK was in the South East (78.2%), while the lowest was in the North East (71.5%); the highest unemployment rate was in London (6.5%), while the lowest was in Northern Ireland (1.8%); the highest economic inactivity rate was in Northern Ireland (26.5%), while the lowest was in the South East (18.5%), in March to May 2026.
notes: Open Government Licence v3.0. ONS flags LFS employment, unemployment and inactivity as official statistics in development, not accredited. Ranges quoted in the body are the ONS figures themselves, not analyst-computed spreads.

title: Labour shortages and surpluses in Europe 2025
date_evidence:
Last update date:

8 June 2026

Published date:

8 June 2026
key_claim: Around one quarter of European employment, 53 million workers, sits in occupations that are in widespread shortage or widespread surplus, and the same occupation is frequently in shortage in one country and in surplus in another.
frame_summary: Europe's shortage problem and its surplus problem are the same problem seen from two places, coexisting occupation by occupation and country by country rather than resolving into one national labour-market state.
verbatim_quote: Around one quarter of employment (53 million workers) is in occupations with widespread shortages or surpluses.
verbatim_list: Surpluses (2 177) are more geographically concentrated and often affect clerical and elementary occupations. Importantly, many occupations appear in shortage in some countries and surplus in others, indicating untapped potential for cross-border labour matching.

While the number of widespread shortage occupations, that is, those reported by more than half of countries, has declined, their severity has increased, suggesting shortages are becoming more concentrated and critical.
notes: The '2025' in the title is the data year; publication date is 8 June 2026, confirmed by the Published date field and the 2026-06 asset path. The final clause of the surpluses quote ('untapped potential for cross-border labour matching') cuts against the signal and is used as a secondary counter-point.

title: State Employment and Unemployment, April 2026
date_evidence: For release 10:00 a.m. (ET) Friday, May 22, 2026                                       USDL-26-0762
key_claim: In April 2026 US state jobless rates ran from 2.2% in South Dakota to 6.2% in the District of Columbia against a national rate of 4.3%, with 17 states below the national figure and 6 states plus DC above it.
frame_summary: The single US national unemployment rate conceals a four-point spread across states that has persisted through a period of national stability.
verbatim_quote:
South Dakota had the lowest jobless rate in April, 2.2 percent, followed by North Dakota, 2.4
percent. The District of Columbia had the highest unemployment rate, 6.2 percent.
verbatim_list: The national unemployment rate, 4.3 percent, was unchanged over the month and was little changed from April 2025.
notes: laus.nr0.htm is the rolling current-release URL; at verification it served the April 2026 release issued 22 May 2026. Line break inside the verbatim quote reflects the fixed-width release text and is normalised by the provenance audit.

title: Labour Market Briefing: July 2026
key_claim: There are now around 5.4 people seeking work for every UK vacancy, yet beneath that national slack city employment rates run from 63.7% in Blackburn to 85.5% in Worthing against a UK rate of 75.4%.
frame_summary: National labour-market aggregates have barely shifted while masking geographical inequalities large enough that employment support now has to be paired with regional economic development rather than national levers.
verbatim_quote: According to Centre for Cities data while the UK employment rate stood at 75.4% in 2025, city employment rates ranged from 63.7% in Blackburn to 85.5% in Worthing.
verbatim_list: As a result, there are now around 5.4 people seeking work for every vacancy. The contrast with the labour shortages seen in 2021 and 2022 is stark: vacancies have fallen steadily from their peak while the pool of people wanting work has grown.
notes: UK independent policy and research institute (charity no. 1002775). The Blackburn/Worthing range is Centre for Cities 2025 city-level data, a different geography and vintage from the ONS region/nation table, so the two ranges are cited separately and not blended. This briefing is L&W's same-day analysis of the 21 July ONS release and is not presented as independent corroboration of ONS.

title: A Shifting Pipeline: What Indeed's Data Reveals About Immigrants' Role in the US Labor Force
key_claim: US net international migration peaked at nearly 2.7 million in 2024 and is projected to fall to 321,000 by mid-2026, a decline of nearly 90% in two years; the share of clicks on US job postings originating abroad has fallen to 1.4% as of April 2026.
frame_summary: The inflow that has been doing the heavy lifting for US labour-force growth is collapsing, removing the national lever firms and policymakers have leaned on to fill shortages.
verbatim_quote: After increasing each year since 2020, net international migration peaked at nearly 2.7 million in 2024. According to the Census Bureau, it is now projected to fall to 321,000 by mid-2026, a decline of nearly 90% in two years.
verbatim_list: The share of clicks on US job postings from abroad peaked in 2023 and has been falling sharply since, sitting at just 1.4% as of April 2026, the lowest value since January 2020.
notes: Indeed's economic research arm, US edition. Author Sneha Puri. National and occupational only, with no state or metro breakdown, so it is not cited for any US geographic claim.

title: Changing Work/Places: Remote Work and the Prospect of Rural and Coastal Revival in Great Britain
key_claim: Fully remote jobs are only 12% of workers, and while that minority does show inter-regional migration, the dominant hybrid mode keeps workers tethered to metropolitan labour markets, so remote work reinforces rather than redraws economic geography.
frame_summary: Remote work consolidates the existing economic geography rather than redrawing it, so hybrid working will not rebalance the UK economy.
verbatim_quote: Perhaps the most important takeaway is this: Remote work is reinforcing existing economic geography—not reshaping it.
verbatim_list: Fully remote jobs are still a minority (12% of workers)

As a result, hybrid working does not fuel migration or noticeable residential relocation. On a smaller scale, we rather see that digital flexibility is used to access new opportunities while staying put.
notes: Author Darja Reuschke (City-REDI, University of Birmingham). Plain-language write-up of the peer-reviewed open-access paper Reuschke & MacLeavy, Regional Science Policy & Practice 18(7):100319, DOI 10.1016/j.rspp.2026.100319. The ScienceDirect page is bot-protected and returns an empty body, so the university blog is cited instead; treat_directionally reflects that. Blog carries a posted date of 16/06/2026 and a modified date of 14/07/2026.

title: Why Americans aren't moving as much as they used to
key_claim: Brookings demographer William Frey: about one-fifth of the US population moved every year in the 1950s, against roughly 9% in the latest year, and the moves that do happen across labour markets are still overwhelmingly job-driven.
frame_summary: Tax-flight narratives are demographically trivial; the real story is a multi-decade collapse in Americans' willingness and ability to relocate, even though jobs remain the dominant motive when they do move.
verbatim_quote: Well, if you look at this historically and go back to the 1950s, about one-fifth of the population moved every year. It's now down to, I think in this last year, it's maybe 9% rather than 20%.
verbatim_list: Well, when they move across state lines or across metropolitan areas — or labor markets, as we might say — they're moving for labor kinds of reasons: to get a new job, because they're transferred, or maybe they think they're going to get a job in this other place. That's a big part of that movement.
notes: Structural anchor: the single source permitted in the 3-6 month band. Marketplace Morning Report; interviewee William Frey, senior fellow, Brookings Institution. The 9% figure is Frey's spoken, hedged estimate and is attributed to Frey in the body, not to the Census Bureau.
